title: BAR U2·W1 — Cost Accounting & Managerial Analysis (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — what a job actually costs

BAR's business-analysis area tests the cost accounting that drives MBG's bids and margins. Before you can analyze a contractor's profitability you must know how costs are classified, accumulated into jobs, and behaved as volume changes. This week builds the costing systems, cost-volume-profit analysis, and standard-cost variances that turn raw spending into decision-useful numbers.

Classifying costs

Costs are sorted several ways. Product costs (direct materials, direct labor, manufacturing overhead) attach to the output and sit in inventory until sold; period costs (selling, general, and administrative) are expensed as incurred. Costs are also direct (traceable to a cost object) or indirect (allocated), and by behavior — variable (changes with volume), fixed (constant in total within the relevant range), or mixed. For decisions, the only costs that matter are relevant — future costs that differ between alternatives; sunk costs are ignored.

Job-order versus process costing

The accumulation system fits the production. Job-order costing traces costs to distinct jobs — perfect for a contractor, where each project (the cost object) accumulates its own materials, labor, and applied overhead. Process costing averages costs over homogeneous mass-produced units, computing equivalent units of production (partially complete units expressed as whole units) under the weighted-average or FIFO method. Overhead is applied using a predetermined rate (budgeted overhead ÷ budgeted activity), with any over- or under-applied overhead closed to cost of goods sold at period end.

Activity-based costing

Activity-based costing (ABC) improves overhead allocation by assigning costs to activities (setups, inspections, material handling) and then to products using cost drivers that cause the activity. ABC is more accurate than a single plant-wide rate when products consume overhead in different proportions than the volume base — it stops high-volume simple products from subsidizing low-volume complex ones. The trade-off is cost and complexity, so ABC is used where overhead is large and diverse.

Cost-volume-profit analysis

CVP analysis links cost, volume, and profit through the contribution margin (sales − variable costs), the amount each sale contributes to covering fixed costs and then profit. The break-even point in units = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit; in dollars = fixed costs ÷ the contribution-margin ratio. Worked example: fixed costs of $300,000 and a $50 contribution margin per unit break even at 6,000 units; to earn a $100,000 target profit requires ($300,000 + $100,000) ÷ $50 = 8,000 units. The margin of safety (actual minus break-even sales) and operating leverage (contribution margin ÷ operating income) measure how sensitive profit is to a sales change.

Absorption versus variable costing

Two costing philosophies treat fixed manufacturing overhead differently. Absorption (full) costing — required for GAAP and tax — treats fixed overhead as a product cost that stays in inventory until sold. Variable (direct) costing — for internal use — expenses fixed overhead as a period cost. The result: when production exceeds sales, absorption income is higher (fixed overhead is deferred in inventory), and the difference reverses when sales exceed production. Reconciling the two is a classic exam computation.

Standard costs and variances

A standard cost system sets expected prices and quantities and analyzes the variances from actual (the foundation laid in BAR Unit 1). Direct cost variances split into price/rate and quantity/efficiency; overhead is analyzed more finely. The four-variance overhead method computes a variable-overhead spending and efficiency variance and a fixed-overhead budget (spending) and volume variance. The volume variance — fixed overhead applied versus budgeted — measures capacity utilization and has no cash effect; it simply reflects producing above or below the level used to set the rate.

Joint products, by-products, and spoilage

When a single process yields multiple outputs, joint costs incurred before the split-off point are allocated among joint products — usually by relative sales value at split-off (or net realizable value), sometimes by physical units. A minor by-product is often credited against the main product's cost. Spoilage is split into normal (inherent in the process — a product cost spread over good units) and abnormal (avoidable — a period loss recognized separately). Each rule keeps inventory and cost of goods sold faithful when production is messy.

Service-department allocation and decision analysis

Overhead from service departments (maintenance, IT) is allocated to operating departments by the direct, step-down, or reciprocal method — the reciprocal method being the most accurate because it recognizes services the departments provide to each other. Cost data also feeds short-run decision analysis: a special order is accepted if its price exceeds the incremental (relevant) cost, even below full cost, when capacity is idle; a make-or-buy decision compares the avoidable cost of making to the purchase price plus the opportunity cost of the freed capacity; and a keep-or-drop decision turns on whether a segment's contribution margin covers its avoidable fixed costs. The unifying rule is that only future costs that differ between alternatives are relevant — allocated common costs and sunk costs are ignored.

Quality and constraint costs

Modern cost management tracks the cost of quality in four buckets — prevention and appraisal (conformance costs spent to avoid defects) versus internal and external failure (nonconformance costs of defects caught before or after delivery) — the insight being that spending on prevention usually lowers total quality cost. The theory of constraints focuses improvement on the bottleneck resource, maximizing throughput (sales minus direct materials) per unit of the constraint. For a contractor, the scarce resource is often skilled crews or key equipment, so scheduling around that constraint drives profitability more than shaving unit costs elsewhere.

A worked equivalent-units calculation

Process costing's signature computation is equivalent units. Suppose a department finishes 17,000 units and leaves 3,000 units 60% complete in ending work in process. Under the weighted-average method, equivalent units = units completed (17,000) + ending WIP × completion (3,000 × 60% = 1,800) = 18,800 equivalent units, and the cost per equivalent unit = total costs (beginning WIP + costs added) ÷ 18,800. The FIFO method instead isolates the work done this period — the effort to finish beginning WIP, plus units started and completed, plus ending WIP's progress. Either way, the equivalent-unit cost is applied to units transferred out and to ending inventory — the mechanism that values partially complete production.

CMA bridge

CMA months 3 and 4 built this cost-management toolkit for MBG; BAR tests it at exam depth and ties it to the financial-analysis ratios from BAR Unit 1. Job-order costing is exactly how MBG accumulates construction costs into the WIP that FAR's percentage-of-completion then recognizes — cost accounting is where the construction numbers begin.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify costs: product vs period, direct vs indirect, variable/fixed/mixed, relevant vs sunk.
  2. Use job-order costing for distinct projects and process costing (equivalent units) for mass production; apply overhead with a predetermined rate and close over/under-applied to COGS.
  3. Compute CVP: break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin; reconcile absorption vs variable costing.
  4. Analyze four-variance overhead (variable spending/efficiency; fixed budget/volume); allocate joint costs by relative sales value and split normal vs abnormal spoilage.

Recap: cost accounting classifies and accumulates costs — job-order for a contractor, process costing with equivalent units for mass output, and ABC when overhead is diverse; CVP finds the break-even (fixed costs ÷ contribution margin, so $300,000 ÷ $50 = 6,000 units); absorption costing defers fixed overhead in inventory while variable costing expenses it; and four-variance analysis plus joint-cost allocation and spoilage rules complete the managerial toolkit.

questions.q: A construction contractor accumulating costs by project uses:
questions.explain: Distinct projects are cost objects under job-order costing; process costing suits homogeneous mass production.

questions.q: The break-even point in units equals:
choices: Fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit
questions.explain: Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit.

questions.q: Fixed costs $300,000, contribution margin $50/unit. Units to earn a $100,000 target profit:

choices: Assigning overhead to activities via cost drivers
questions.explain: ABC traces overhead to activities and then to products through cost drivers.

questions.q: When production exceeds sales, absorption-costing net income compared with variable costing is:
questions.explain: Absorption defers fixed overhead in ending inventory, raising income relative to variable costing.

questions.q: Joint costs incurred before the split-off point are most commonly allocated by:
questions.explain: Relative sales value (or NRV) at split-off is the usual joint-cost allocation base.

choices: A product cost spread over good units
questions.explain: Normal spoilage is inherent and absorbed into the cost of good units; abnormal spoilage is a separate period loss.
